fields.label: Table — 8 rows
rows: Dust boots and covers where fatigue life governs and there is no oil contact
Protective boots exposed to weather, ozone and moderate oil together
Boots and bellows in contact with petroleum oils and hydraulic fluid
Water, steam, coolant and weather-exposed bellows. Not for petroleum oils
Under-bonnet bellows where oil, heat and ozone act together
Chemical and fuel-contact bellows at sustained high temperature
Low-cost covers in water and mild service. Not for oil or fuel
High-temperature bellows where movement is limited. Poor tear and fatigue resistance
fields.note: Eight rows, up from four. Natural rubber leads because it has the best flex-fatigue resistance of any of these families and is absent from the live table entirely; neoprene is second because it is the classic protective-boot compound and is also absent. Every temperature range matches the homepage compound table, which governs across all eleven category pages. Both were settled on the homepage sheet, 2026-09-03, and the resolution is carried here — FKM publishes +250 °C with continuous to +200 °C beneath it, AEM +175 °C with continuous to +160 °C. The peak stays the headline figure and the continuous figure is stated. The remaining question is a grade question for Margo, not a table question

fields.label: Footnote
paragraphs: Showing 8 of 8 entries. Flex-fatigue resistance is a relative ranking between compound families, not a cycle count. Cycle life for a given part depends on stroke, convolution geometry, wall thickness, installed pre-load and temperature as much as on the compound, and is established by qualification testing on that part — to ISO 132, ASTM D430 or ASTM D813 — not read off a table. Tell us the stroke and the target cycle life and we will qualify against it. Ranges are typical values for the compound family and are not a specification for a particular part; see our technical disclaimer.
leads: Flex-fatigue resistance is a relative ranking between compound families, not a cycle count.
marked: Showing 8 of 8 entries. **Flex-fatigue resistance is a relative ranking between compound families, not a cycle count.** Cycle life for a given part depends on stroke, convolution geometry, wall thickness, installed pre-load and temperature as much as on the compound, and is established by qualification testing on that part — to ISO 132, ASTM D430 or ASTM D813 — not read off a table. **Tell us the stroke and the target cycle life and we will qualify against it.** Ranges are typical values for the compound family and are not a specification for a particular part; see our technical disclaimer.
fields.note: 84 words · live is 26 · the longest footnote in the set, and the one doing the most work. It is what converts an unsupportable number into a defensible position, and the offer in bold is the part that opens an enquiry. This is the paragraph that removes the rubric cap on this section

notes: Real <table> markup with <caption>Bellows compounds, flex-fatigue behaviour and service temperatures</caption> and scope="col" on every header. All eight rows in the DOM at first paint; filter with CSS, never unmount.

This table is the page’s AEO surface, and after the rewrite it answers a question almost nothing else on the internet answers plainly: “which rubber compound lasts longest in a flexing boot”. Distributors publish size charts; nobody publishes fatigue ranking with the test method named.

Naming ISO 132, ASTM D430 and ASTM D813 is the credibility move. It shows the fatigue question is understood properly, which is a stronger signal to an engineer than a number would have been — and unlike the number, it is true.

Do not put the fatigue ranking in schema. Visible copy only. A machine-readable fatigue property gets quoted without the footnote that qualifies it, which recreates the problem the footnote exists to solve.
Overflow. Four columns will not fit 375 px — overflow-x:auto on the wrapper, never on the body.

Link the disclaimer beneath the table, anchor text technical disclaimer → /legal/disclaimer. That page carries eight placeholder sections while this table publishes engineering guidance; the full copy is written in sheet 08.

fields.note: 42 words · live is 27 · the live intro says “pressure class”, which is a flange-gasket concept inherited from the template. On a bellows the second axis is stroke and cycle count, and naming it correctly is what tells an engineer the page was written by someone who has made one

fields.label: Panels ×8
rows: Polyisoprene. The best flex-fatigue resistance of the eight and the highest resilience, which is why it is specified for dust boots and covers that flex for the life of the vehicle. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Polychloroprene. The classic protective boot compound — it holds weather, ozone and moderate oil exposure at the same time, which is the condition most exposed boots actually live in. Also the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.

Nitrile butadiene rubber, the general-purpose industry standard. Outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and hydraulic fluids at moderate temperature, and the usual answer for a bellows on the oil side of an assembly.

Ethylene propylene diene rubber, the preferred material for water, steam, coolant and brake fluid service, with excellent weather and ozone resistance. Holds a convolution outdoors for years. Not for petroleum oils.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications. Specified for under-bonnet bellows where oil, heat and ozone act together — the combination that ends most boots.

Fluorocarbon rubber, the first choice for aggressive chemical environments. Resists petroleum oils, fuels and many solvents at sustained high temperature. Specify it for chemistry and heat rather than for flex life.
Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, for covers and boots in water and mild service. Not for oil or fuel contact.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Biocompatible and food-contact grades on request. Poor tear and abrasion resistance, so specify it for temperature rather than for a bellows that flexes hard.
fields.note: Eight panels. Panel order leads with natural rubber and neoprene — the two compounds a flexing part is most often made from, and the two the live page omits entirely. The live order leads with FKM, which on a bellows is the specialist answer, not the default. Every range matches the homepage compound table. Body copy for the four live panels is kept close to the original where it is accurate; each gains a bellows-specific closing clause, because the same paragraph currently renders on eleven category pages and says nothing about any of them

fields.label: Panel link
fields.note: [no change to the label]. It expands the panel in place; it does not navigate. Keep it a <button>, not an <a>

notes: Crawlability. All eight panels render in the DOM at first paint and collapse with CSS. An accordion that mounts its body on click publishes eight paragraphs to a browser and zero to a crawler — the most common way a well-written technical page scores nothing.
Heading levels. Section heading is <h2>; each compound name is <h3> inside the panel. Eight <h3>s under one question <h2> is a clean, extractable outline.
The H2 is a literal buyer question, which is the AEO pattern. The passage under it answers in the first 40 to 60 words, before the accordion starts — which is what the rewritten intro does.

The compound-specific closing clauses are what make this page rankable. Identical body copy on eleven category pages is eleven pages of duplicate content competing with each other; the closing clause is the only thing distinguishing this page’s NBR panel from the O-rings page’s NBR panel.

FAQ schema. This section feeds two of the four FAQPage questions: “Which rubber compound is best for a flexing bellows?” and “What temperature can an EPDM bellows withstand?”. Answer text must match the visible copy word for word.

Shared component, one data source. The compound data should come from one file, not eleven hand-maintained copies — that is how four temperature ranges came to disagree with the homepage on four separate category pages.
